The Lowland burrowing tree frog Smilisca fodiens is a fossorial hylid that inhabits arid and semi-arid lowlands of western Mexico. Newly hatched individuals emerge from their gelatinous egg masses at a remarkably small size, with a wet weight at birth of just 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams], a value derived from the average egg diameter of two millimeters. This minuscule neonatal mass reflects the species strategy of producing large clutches of small, rapidly developing eggs in ephemeral pools. Under controlled laboratory conditions set at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the embryos complete development and undergo eclosion after a brief incubation period of approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days]. This rapid developmental rate is an adaptation to the unpredictable availability of breeding sites, where water bodies may persist for only a few weeks. Following the rupture of the jelly capsule, the newly emerged tadpoles are lecithotrophic and depend entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves during the first few days before transitioning to active filter feeding on suspended algae and detritus in the warm, shallow pools they occupy.

The tadpole phase in Smilisca fodiens proceeds through a series of Gosner stages characterized by steady somatic growth and progressive morphological differentiation. The entire larval period culminates in metamorphic climax, during which the gill-breathing larva undergoes a dramatic body plan reorganisation, including tail resorption and limb development. Field observations indicate that the time from hatching to the completion of metamorphosis, when the juvenile froglet first emerges onto land, is approximately 21 days  when development occurs at a stable water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This relatively short larval duration is typical of species breeding in temporary aquatic habitats, where desiccation risk imposes strong selection for rapid development. Following metamorphosis, the newly terrestrial juveniles weigh only a fraction of a gram and must quickly secure invertebrate prey to fuel their continued growth.

Following metamorphosis, the post-metamorphic juveniles enter a period of rapid mass gain during which they forage actively on small arthropods in the leaf litter. As they approach reproductive maturity, the females in particular undergo substantial increases in body size. The ultimate wet weight attained by adult females in this species averages 15.1 grams [Wwi = 15.1 grams], a body mass that represents an enormous increase from the 0.0042 gram neonate. This large adult size likely facilitates the production of sizeable clutches during the brief breeding season. The onset of gonadal maturation, marked by the first development of vitellogenic oocytes in the ovaries, occurs considerably later. Measurements from captive populations reared at 27 °C [T = 27 °C] indicate that the time since metamorphosis at which females first reach puberty is approximately 3 years [tp = approximately 3 years], a substantial delay reflecting the energetic demands of reaching an adequate body size before reproductive allocation can commence.

The reproductive output of Smilisca fodiens females is closely tied to the brief window of suitable conditions following heavy rains. During a single breeding event, gravid females deposit their eggs in amplexus within a foam nest constructed on the water's surface. Each clutch typically contains between 100 and 200 eggs [N_R_i = Each clutch typically contains between 100 and 200 eggs], a modest fecundity for a hylid of its body size. Because the breeding season is restricted to a few weeks during the rainy period, most females are capable of producing only a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], meaning their annual reproductive output is limited to the contents of that single nest. Under optimal thermal conditions maintained at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the maximum annual reproductive output inferred from this clutch size and frequency is limited to the contents of that single nest, a pattern consistent with the life history of a species that invests in a small number of large eggs per event rather than continuous, high-frequency spawning.

Longevity data for Smilisca fodiens remain sparse, but mark-recapture studies of a population in Jalisco have provided some initial estimates. The oldest documented individual in the wild was a female recaptured approximately 1860 days after her initial marking as a recently metamorphosed juvenile, indicating a maximum lifespan of about 5.1 years [am = about 5.1 years] when development and adult activity occur at 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. Resting metabolic rate measurements, conducted via closed-system respirometry on post-absorptive individuals at a controlled temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], yielded a maximum basal oxygen consumption of 0.0081 milliliters per hour [JOi = 0.0081 milliliters per hour]. This extremely low metabolic rate is consistent with the fossorial lifestyle of the species, as burrowing amphibians typically exhibit reduced energy expenditures compared to their surface-dwelling relatives, enabling them to persist through extended dry periods in underground retreats where food availability is limited.
